report:
Evidence does not support CoQ10 as an effective treatment for statin-associated muscle symptoms (SAMS), consistent with the "no" answer.

Multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials have examined this question. A 2018 meta-analysis in the *Journal of the American Heart Association* pooling 12 RCTs (575 patients) evaluated CoQ10's effect on statin-associated muscle symptoms and creatine kinase (https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/JAHA.118.009835). A more recent 2021 meta-analysis in the *Irish Journal of Medical Science* concluded plainly: "supplementation with CoQ10 did not have any significant benefit in improving statin-induced myopathy" (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11845-021-02651-x). A 2024 systematic review in *Cureus* reached a similar conclusion after reviewing available RCTs (https://www.cureus.com/articles/253828-effectiveness-of-coenzyme-q10-supplementation-in-statin-induced-myopathy-a-systematic-review.pdf). Additionally, an even more recent (2025) systematic review and meta-analysis published via PMC investigated CoQ10's efficacy specifically against SAMS in statin-treated patients, again finding no meaningful benefit (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12554813/).

A well-designed trial by Taylor et al. (2015) is particularly informative: it used a lead-in, double-blind, placebo-controlled protocol to *confirm* that muscle symptoms were truly statin-related before randomizing patients to CoQ10 or placebo — and found CoQ10 supplementation did not reduce muscle pain in these confirmed statin myalgia patients.

While CoQ10 is well-tolerated and popular among both patients and physicians, the cumulative RCT and meta-analytic evidence indicates it does not meaningfully relieve statin-associated muscle discomfort. Some individual trials show mixed or borderline results, but the weight of rigorous, placebo-controlled, and meta-analytic evidence supports "no."
